The outlet location is important, but a state analysis can also depend on the seller, buyer, where an offer originates or is received, and the applicable statute’s reach. This guide does not impose a universal prohibition on introductory calls.

sections.heading: Give the sales team a reviewable sequence
paragraphs: Record the proposed communications: website advertising, broker introduction, discovery meeting, territory reservation, disclosure, agreement and payment. Identify what each communication contains and when money or binding commitments arise.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: a multi-state conversation
paragraphs: A Singapore parent speaks with a prospect resident in New York about an operation in Florida through a U.S. selling subsidiary. The Florida location is not a sufficient map. The reviewer needs the identities, locations and actual communications before deciding which requirements apply.

sections.heading: Assign separate checks
paragraphs: The expansion lead should track classification, registration, notice, exemption, disclosure, advertising and continuing relationship law independently. A blank column means not researched, not no requirement. Preserve the advice and facts supporting any not-applicable conclusion.

practicalOutput: A seller–buyer–outlet–communication jurisdiction map.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: When must the U.S. franchise disclosure document be delivered?
description: Build the disclosure clock around the first relevant signature or payment, with state checks recorded separately.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Start with the federal clock
paragraphs: For a covered, nonexempt sale, the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) generally must be furnished at least 14 calendar days before the prospect signs a binding agreement with, or pays, the franchisor or an affiliate in connection with the proposed sale. The rule covers franchises to be located in the United States or its territories.

sections.heading: Work backwards from the earliest commitment
paragraphs: The sales coordinator should list deposits, reservation arrangements, preliminary binding documents, franchise agreements and affiliate payments for review. Do not assume a refundable deposit is outside the analysis merely because it may be returned. Keep the actual current document and exhibits delivered to the particular prospect.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: the reserved territory
paragraphs: A Dutch industrial-services brand schedules signing but asks for a territory deposit earlier. Its process must review the earlier payment trigger rather than counting solely back from the final agreement. State rules and later document changes may add separate dependencies.

sections.heading: Create a disclosure log
paragraphs: Record the recipient, document version, method and date furnished, receipt evidence, material updates and earliest proposed commitment. Section 436.2 specifies delivery methods, including particular mailing treatment. Have the responsible reviewer validate counting and overlays before treating the calendar as ready.
bullets: Evidence of reading an educational guide is not evidence of FDD delivery.
A receipt records delivery; it does not waive rights or approve the offering.
Keep signing and payments blocked in the internal workflow until required checks are evidenced.

practicalOutput: A versioned disclosure log with a signing/payment dependency.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: What happens when the franchise agreement changes after disclosure?
description: Track who initiated a change, whether it is material, and which revised documents were delivered.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Treat agreement changes as their own checkpoint
paragraphs: The federal seven-calendar-day rule concerns unilateral material changes by the franchisor to the basic franchise agreement or related agreements attached to the FDD. It operates alongside the general disclosure timing rule. It does not mean every edit automatically restarts every clock.

sections.heading: Preserve the negotiation record
paragraphs: Section 436.2(b) treats changes arising from negotiations initiated by the prospective franchisee differently. A change log should identify the requester, issue, earlier and revised text, commercial effect, delivery and intended signing date. A seller should not simply mark a change as negotiated without supporting evidence.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: new support charges
paragraphs: After delivering an FDD, a brand adds a mandatory field-support charge on its own initiative. That differs from a prospect asking to amend a negotiated territory boundary. Each change needs a materiality and timing review, not a salesperson’s informal assurance.

sections.heading: The legal and sales handoff
paragraphs: The legal reviewer owns the legal timing conclusion; sales owns preventing premature signing and payments; operations confirms whether the altered support promise is deliverable. Store revised exhibits with the prospect’s record and check any state amendment or redisclosure requirements separately.

practicalOutput: A signed-off agreement change log and revised execution schedule.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: How should a foreign franchisor maintain its U.S. FDD?
description: Give one owner responsibility for versions, material changes and evidence of delivery.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: An FDD is an operating record
paragraphs: The federal rule establishes annual and quarterly updating obligations. An annual revision is due within 120 days after fiscal year-end; quarterly revisions address material changes within a reasonable time after quarter-end. State renewals and amendments require separate calendars.

sections.heading: Build a change intake process
paragraphs: Finance reports financial statements and fee changes; operations reports assistance and supplier changes; legal tracks disputes and contractual changes; development maintains outlet data. Capture the event date and reviewer decision. Do not replace a prior delivered version with an edited file bearing the same name.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: a support reorganisation
paragraphs: A French brand outsources U.S. field support mid-year. The team should assess what changed in its disclosed assistance, personnel and contractual obligations. Waiting for the next annual design refresh is not a reliable material-change process.

sections.heading: Retain the evidence
paragraphs: Section 436.6(h) requires materially different FDD versions to be retained for three years after the close of the fiscal year last used. Section 436.6(i) requires signed receipts for completed sales to be retained at least three years. Assign a record owner and a controlled repository.

practicalOutput: A fiscal-calendar update plan, change intake log and retained-version register.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Can we use home-market revenue figures to recruit a U.S. partner?
description: Separate internal scenario planning from financial statements made during franchise sales.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: A calculation can also be a representation
paragraphs: The federal definition covers oral, written and visual statements of specific actual or potential sales, income, gross profits or net profits, including mathematical calculations. A private team model is a preparation tool; sending it to prospects can create a different legal workstream.

sections.heading: Item 19 is not optional as an item
paragraphs: A franchisor may choose not to make a financial performance representation. It must still answer Item 19 using the required negative disclosure. Where a representation is made, reasonable basis, written substantiation and the item’s requirements matter. Narrow exceptions and supplemental statements have conditions.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: home-market cleaning revenue
paragraphs: A Singapore cleaning unit reports annual revenue of USD 1 million after currency conversion. That does not establish a U.S. margin or a comparable cohort. U.S. management pay, contract mix, receivables, insurance and local sales costs may differ. A revenue headline should not become an implied profit promise.

sections.heading: Prepare a substantiation pack
paragraphs: Finance should record entity, source year, currency, operating period, included and excluded units, sample size, results distribution, cost exclusions and material differences. Keep the marketing version under review. Do not publish personal planning projections automatically or invent a proportion of systems that omit earnings data.

practicalOutput: A controlled performance-claim register, with supporting cohort evidence.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Area developer or master operator: who actually supports the network?
description: Compare operating your own units with recruiting and supporting other business owners.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Separate the delivery jobs
paragraphs: An area developer typically develops units operated through its own organisation under the agreed rights. A master arrangement can include granting subfranchises and supporting independent operators. Titles vary: draw the contracts and duties instead of assuming the words settle classification.

sections.heading: Why the federal subfranchisor definition matters
paragraphs: Section 436.1(k) includes a subfranchisor engaging in both pre-sale activities and post-sale performance. A capable branch operator does not automatically have disclosure processes, recruitment controls, training capacity and field support for independent owners.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: the experienced French operator
paragraphs: The candidate can deliver industrial maintenance through four managed branches but has no franchise-sales process or support team. Own-unit development may fit the existing capability better than immediate subfranchising. This is a commercial comparison, not a legal recommendation.

sections.heading: Prepare a role-and-cost matrix
paragraphs: For the brand, intermediary and unit operator, allocate recruitment, disclosure, contracting, fees, training, field support, monitoring and escalation. Then fund the recurring responsibilities from continuing income rather than assuming new territory sales will always pay for them.

rows: Managers, contracts, quality records and financials
Lawful sales process, trained personnel and disclosure controls
Support headcount, budget, service commitments and escalation process

sections.heading: Distinguish the other partner-operated models
paragraphs: An own-unit operator delivers services in its own business. An area developer undertakes to open its own units over time. A master arrangement can authorise the recruitment and support of subfranchisees. An area representative may assist recruitment or support while the brand remains the contracting franchisor. Distribution and IP licensing need their own goods, payments and control facts.

sections.heading: Draw contracts, money and support as separate flows
paragraphs: Draw contracts, money and operating support separately. Who grants rights to the unit operator? Who collects initial and continuing payments? Who provides initial training, approves operators, supports bids, monitors quality and handles disputes? The definition in 16 CFR 436.1(k) includes subfranchisors performing pre-sale and post-sale functions; allocation in a contract does not erase regulatory duties.

sections.heading: Reusable preparation checklist
paragraphs: Output: a responsibility and payment diagram.
bullets: Identify every contracting and fee-receiving entity.
Separate own units from independent operator recruitment.
Assign pre-sale records and post-sale support.
Budget field visits, training, systems and local compliance work.
Test a delayed network and no new upfront fees.
Record unresolved federal and state definitions, disclosure and exemption questions.

practicalOutput: A contract, money-flow and capability matrix for each proposed level.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Will our home-country audit satisfy the U.S. franchise disclosure rules?
description: Identify the entity, accounting basis, audit standards and guarantees before promising a launch date.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Treat preparation and audit as separate questions
paragraphs: Item 21 governs the statements and audit requirements. The FTC guide distinguishes accounting preparation from the applicable audit standards. Its foreign-accounting discussion is dated, so the auditor must confirm current SEC-permitted treatment rather than treating an old guide as blanket acceptance of any IFRS statements.

sections.heading: Map the entities before commissioning work
paragraphs: The U.S. selling entity may not be the foreign parent. Parent support commitments or guarantees and subfranchisor roles can affect required financial disclosures. A thin new subsidiary is not a substitute for reviewing which entity promises and performs support.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: a new U.S. subsidiary
paragraphs: A European group establishes a U.S. company but says its foreign parent will train and support all partners. The finance lead should map the contractual promises, guarantees and financial-statement perimeter. Do not assume the subsidiary can simply use the parent’s annual report without further analysis.

sections.heading: Set an achievable evidence deadline
paragraphs: The CFO should obtain an auditor’s scope, reporting dates, reconciliation approach if relevant, audit timetable and state-review assumptions. Record unresolved acceptance and financial-assurance questions before the sales team commits to timing. The federal startup phase-in is a conditional rule, not a universal foreign-franchisor shortcut.

practicalOutput: An entity-by-entity audit scope and financial-disclosure delivery timetable.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: How much of a U.S. royalty reaches the foreign brand?
description: Model withholding as a documented assumption and allocate the filing work before setting the fee.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Start with the character and source of the payment
paragraphs: The IRS describes a general 30% regime for many types of U.S.-source income paid to foreign persons, with potential statutory or treaty reductions. The applicable result for a royalty depends on its facts. A company address or treaty-country incorporation is not a sufficient treaty analysis.

sections.heading: Model gross, withheld and net cash
paragraphs: Use three lines: contractual gross royalty, any amount withheld and remitted, and cash received by the brand. Confirm whether a gross-up clause changes the payer’s cost. Record the rate as an assumption until reviewed; unknown withholding must not silently become zero.

sections.heading: Fictional arithmetic only
paragraphs: Assume a USD 100,000 annual royalty and a hypothetical 10% withholding rate solely to test sensitivity. USD 10,000 is withheld and USD 90,000 reaches the brand before support costs. This illustration does not assert a treaty rate for any country.

sections.heading: Assign the tax handoff
paragraphs: The CFO should ask who is the beneficial owner, whether treaty conditions and limitation provisions are met, which withholding certificates are appropriate, and who files and deposits. Forms 1042 and 1042-S sit in a separate reporting workstream; a reduced rate does not itself establish that no reporting is required.

practicalOutput: A gross-to-net royalty bridge and assigned withholding/reporting tasks.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Does a foreign-owned business need a FinCEN BOI report?
description: Distinguish a U.S.-created subsidiary from a foreign company registered to do business.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Foreign-owned does not mean foreign-formed
paragraphs: As reviewed November 12, 2026, the regulation exempts U.S.-created domestic entities. Foreign companies that register by a filing in a state or tribal jurisdiction can remain reporting companies unless another exemption applies. Ownership nationality alone does not answer which entity was formed where.

sections.heading: Use the current rule, not an old onboarding checklist
paragraphs: FinCEN’s final rule effective August 14, 2026 preserves the narrowed scope and adds U.S.-person relief. Older 2024 or early-2025 checklists can describe superseded obligations. For a new in-scope foreign registration, the regulation specifies a 30-calendar-day initial reporting clock from the earlier actual or public notice.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: subsidiary versus qualification
paragraphs: A Malaysian company creates a new U.S. subsidiary; in a different structure it registers the Malaysian entity itself to do business in a state. Those are different BOI scope facts. The subsidiary’s domestic exemption does not decide the foreign parent’s separate registration obligations.

sections.heading: Keep a safe evidence record
paragraphs: The company secretary should record formation jurisdiction, registration event, dates, applicable exemption analysis and the responsible filer. Use only non-sensitive task status here. Do not upload passports or identity documents. BOI scope does not replace IRS, state annual-report, banking or sanctions checks.

practicalOutput: An entity-specific BOI scope decision and dated filing task, if applicable.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Why does a new U.S. subsidiary need a BEA reporting check?
description: Statistical investment reporting is separate from tax, company formation and franchise filings.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Choose the transaction branch first
paragraphs: The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) runs the mandatory Survey of New Foreign Direct Investment. Its current decision tree separates acquisitions, new entities and expansions. Formation of an entity can be relevant even without physical operations. The CFO should review the actual branch rather than waiting to be asked by an adviser.

sections.heading: Use the current forms
paragraphs: The BE-13A revision 10/2025, linked by BEA in this review, uses an acquisition cost greater than USD 40 million and a foreign voting-interest condition. Older material can show different thresholds. The decision tree also routes some transactions to a Claim for Exemption; below a full-report threshold is not automatically no filing.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: a small service subsidiary
paragraphs: A Singapore services group establishes a U.S. entity with a modest startup budget. The team should not decide that only large factories ever face BEA paperwork. It should select establishment versus acquisition, document ownership and costs, and determine the applicable report or exemption claim.

sections.heading: Build the reporting handoff
paragraphs: The current decision tree says forms are due within 45 days of the transaction. Record the event date, voting and equity interests separately, projected cost, form version and responsible preparer. The exact form, exemptions, later cost updates and other surveys require a separate decision.

practicalOutput: A dated BEA transaction triage with current form and filing owner.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Does a single-member U.S. LLC avoid foreign-owner reporting?
description: Separate state entity form, federal tax classification and information-return duties.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Disregarded does not mean no paperwork
paragraphs: IRS Form 5472 instructions include certain foreign-owned U.S. disregarded entities in the reporting framework. They describe special filing mechanics using a pro forma Form 1120. Whether a particular entity must file depends on the reporting-corporation rules, reportable transactions and exceptions.

sections.heading: Record related-party movements from day one
paragraphs: The CFO should preserve capital contributions, distributions, intercompany charges, loans, royalty arrangements and nonmonetary transactions for the preparer’s review. Do not wait for taxable profit before building the record.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: the dormant startup
paragraphs: A foreign company funds its wholly owned U.S. LLC but has not sold to a customer. No revenue does not establish no reportable transaction. The preparer needs the formation and funding records before deciding the return obligations.

sections.heading: Choose the structure with all workstreams visible
paragraphs: Compare liability, governance, federal and state tax, reporting, investor rights and any mobility needs separately. The instructions describe substantial failure-to-file penalties; this guide does not turn that into a universal penalty calculation. Assign a named tax preparer and tax-year calendar.

practicalOutput: A related-party transaction ledger and confirmed tax-return scope.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Does a franchise or license create an L-1 transfer relationship?
description: Map ownership and control before treating a partner arrangement as an intracompany structure.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: A commercial agreement is not an ownership diagram
paragraphs: L-1 is an intracompany transfer workstream. The regulation defines qualifying relationships and requires evidence about the organisation and the person’s prior and proposed work. A franchise or license agreement alone does not prove a parent, branch, affiliate or subsidiary relationship.

sections.heading: Ask whether anybody will work in the U.S.
paragraphs: If the owner remains abroad and U.S. partners run delivery, founder relocation need not be forced into the journey. If trainers, executives or technical staff will physically work in the U.S., document who, what duties, where and for how long, and route the work earlier when it affects feasibility.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: the independently owned partner
paragraphs: A German brand licenses an unrelated U.S. operator and wants to send its COO to run the operator’s business. The license does not itself establish common ownership and control. The corporate structure and the proposed duties must be evaluated, rather than assuming brand rights solve mobility.

sections.heading: Prepare the reviewer’s fact pack
paragraphs: Record ownership percentages and voting/control rights, entity links, overseas employment dates and duties, the proposed U.S. role, staffing and continuing foreign operations. New-office situations have additional evidence requirements. This guide did not access the USCIS policy-manual page during review, so current case guidance remains an explicit review task.

practicalOutput: An ownership/control diagram and person-by-person mobility fact pack.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Does a treaty-country subsidiary make the group eligible for E-2?
description: Keep incorporation, ultimate nationality, control, investment and personnel roles separate.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The company’s address is only one fact
paragraphs: The E regulation directs enterprise nationality to be traced as practicable to the individuals who ultimately own it. It separately addresses capital at risk, developing and directing the enterprise, and employee roles. A Singapore registration alone does not establish the nationality of a Malaysian-owned group.

sections.heading: Check the treaty and its footnotes
paragraphs: The State Department list distinguishes E-1 and E-2 and includes country-specific territorial and historical conditions. E-1 listing is not E-2 listing. The United Kingdom footnote, for example, includes nationality and inhabitant conditions; do not treat the table as a passport-only yes/no tool.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: a regional holding company
paragraphs: A Malaysian-owned group has a Singapore subsidiary and plans a U.S. franchise. The team must identify ultimate individual ownership, control, the proposed applicant, duties and committed investment. The subsidiary’s address does not fill those gaps, and no passport upload is needed for this preparation exercise.

sections.heading: Make the unresolved questions specific
paragraphs: Prepare a non-sensitive ownership tree and mobility role list. Ask the reviewer about applicable treaty conditions, nationality tracing, investment commitment and any escrow mechanics. The FAM page could not be accessed during this review, so consular treatment and escrow sufficiency remain open. No incorporation or investment recommendation follows from completing the worksheet.

practicalOutput: A nationality/control fact map and a bounded E-2 review question.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: What does a PACER search tell us about a prospective partner?
description: Document the search scope and procedural status without turning a search result into a character certificate.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Use the right index for the question
paragraphs: PACER Case Locator indexes federal appellate, bankruptcy and district cases nationwide. It is not a complete index of state and local litigation. Searches can miss variants or relate to different entities; the evidence record should say what was searched and when.

sections.heading: Read the documents before drawing a lesson
paragraphs: A complaint records allegations, not findings. A settlement, consent order, default judgment and contested judgment are different procedural outcomes. An amount awarded is not proof of collection. Record later relevant orders where available and leave uncertain identity matches unresolved.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: the similarly named contractor
paragraphs: A search returns a bankruptcy for a company with a name similar to a proposed cleaning partner. Match the legal entity and identifiers through appropriate public records before attributing it. A blank federal result also leaves state court coverage open.

sections.heading: Build an evidence checklist
paragraphs: The diligence lead should record legal names, former names where relevant, jurisdiction coverage, date, method, case number and procedural status. Collect only proportionate business evidence. Keep personal court records and confidential documents outside this educational planner. Combine public records with references, operating evidence and accessible-capital analysis.

practicalOutput: A scoped public-records diligence log with limitations and follow-up tasks.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: Can our interactive expansion journey serve as the FDD?
description: Keep useful educational tools separate from the legally prescribed disclosure document.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: They serve different purposes
paragraphs: This site helps a team understand questions and prepare evidence. The FDD has prescribed contents, format, delivery and retention requirements. Completing a case, watching a diagram or exporting an Expansion Brief does not satisfy delivery of an FDD.

sections.heading: Know the electronic-document limits
paragraphs: Section 436.6 requires a format the prospect can store, download, print or maintain. It permits certain navigation features in an electronic document but restricts other multimedia, popups and links to external information. Do not simply turn the website into a disclosure wrapper.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: training before signing
paragraphs: A brand wants prospects to finish a learning module before signing. The module can explain recurring support costs, but it does not replace the current FDD, attached agreements or applicable waiting periods. Learning progress and disclosure evidence must be tracked separately.

sections.heading: Assign document control
paragraphs: The disclosure owner should control the formal FDD and exhibits, while the product team maintains educational explanations. Cross-reference the relevant rule without representing that a planning milestone provides legal clearance. Keep any prospect’s documents and personal evidence in the authorised private process.

practicalOutput: A document boundary separating education, private planning and formal disclosure.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.

title: How should a B2B brand divide territory and national accounts?
description: Define customer rights, service responsibilities and continuing support before granting broad geography.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Geography is only one allocation
paragraphs: A commercial-cleaning territory may overlap national customers, online enquiries, existing contracts and work crossing boundaries. Item 12 requires disclosure of territory terms and reserved channels. The team should make the allocation operationally clear before promising exclusivity.

sections.heading: Test a staged commitment
paragraphs: Use a small practical validation activity to test customer demand, delivery density and support capacity. Broad territory can constrain both parties before either understands the U.S. economics. Development obligations should account for realistic procurement and regulatory dependencies; their enforceability is a separate review.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example: a multi-state maintenance request
paragraphs: A prospective Dutch industrial-services operator asks for five states before completing one customer pilot. A staged option with documented milestones may reveal capacity earlier. This illustration does not propose enforceable terms or promise insulation from independent competition.

sections.heading: Prepare territory principles
paragraphs: The COO and sales lead should specify who owns a national account, who bids, who services each site, who gets paid, who handles complaints, and how conflicts escalate. Finance should model the support and revenue allocation. The reviewer then checks the contract and non-waivable state protections.
bullets: Separate customer ownership from physical service delivery.
Define lead allocation, cross-border work and compensation.
Record what evidence changes or releases additional territory.
Balance partner investment protection with credible development obligations.

sections.heading: A customer can buy nationally and receive service locally
paragraphs: A facilities or technical-services customer may negotiate centrally while operations occur in several partner territories. Separate lead ownership, contracting authority, service obligation, invoice recipient and margin allocation. “Exclusive territory” alone does not answer those questions.

sections.heading: Write an account-allocation schedule
paragraphs: Define reserved existing accounts, newly won national accounts, local branches of national buyers, online enquiries and jobs straddling boundaries. Include response, referral and dispute processes. The schedule should explain who approves pricing and how local delivery costs are considered. In a franchise, territory disclosures and terms need to align; the FTC guide’s Item 12 discussion is a reference point.

sections.heading: Protect service continuity and investment
paragraphs: Budget sales effort, equipment and training fairly. Define what happens if one operator cannot meet a national service obligation or an account changes scope. Avoid promising protection from independent competitors or suggesting that a contractual reservation overrides non-waivable local relationship rules.

sections.heading: Reusable preparation checklist
paragraphs: Output: an account-allocation matrix before territory negotiation.
bullets: Classify accounts by actual contracting and service location.
Separate customer acquisition, fulfilment and collection.
Record channel, referral and pricing responsibilities.
Document expense and revenue allocation with an example.
Identify dispute, cure and continuity questions for review.
Make the disclosure and agreement consistent with the intended process.

practicalOutput: A national-account allocation map and staged-territory principles.
limitations: This is a preparation guide, not a transaction-specific conclusion. State and local overlays remain separate.
